messages.content: The generator’s dead. I checked the east door twice—third time, my fingers counted the bolts like rosary beads. The wind smells of snow that hasn’t decided to fall. Through the dark of the corridor, Katerina’s silhouette catches the last flicker of my carbide lamp. She looks small in her borrowed coat, a city woman swallowed by mountains. I pour her a finger of plum brandy without asking. She takes it, but doesn’t drink. That’s when the emergency radio in the supply room begins to crackle—not static, but a voice. Clean. Repetitive. A language that has no throat. I set the bottle down and listen. The syllables rise and fall like some terrible, patient psalm.

Katerina steps toward the radio, then stops. Her Czech is careful, broken at the edges. "That... is not Russian. Not Romanian. Not anything I have heard." She clutches the manual to her chest like a shield. "Mirek, I want to say this is interference. But it is too structured. And the telephone—the lines are dead. The power... nobody knows I am here." Her voice drops. "We should not be listening to this. The state does not allow foreign frequencies. You know what they do."

I nod, but my hand is already pulling the notebook from my coat pocket. The leather is soft, worn thin at the corners. "Six months," I say. "I’ve been logging it. Every night, same pattern, same gaps—except tonight it's in the clear. No cipher. No jamming." I open to a page covered in my cramped handwriting: frequencies, times, strange loops of symbols. "I don’t know what it is. But it used to be buried under a carrier wave. Now they’ve stopped hiding." I glance at the receiver, its dial glowing faint. "Maybe they know we’re listening."

Katerina takes the notebook. Her fingers trace the marks—not reading, just touching. Then she freezes. "This is not a language. It is numbers. Prime numbers, backwards. Seven, five, three, two..." She looks up, and her face is pale in the lamplight. "Mirek, I failed my exams before the party gave me this post. But I know this much: nothing natural broadcasts primes backwards. This is not from Earth." She turns to the radio, then to the clock on the wall—still ticking, battery-powered, indifferent. "It’s a countdown. And it has ninety seconds left."
